grade6.crumb: ‹ Grade 6 Science · Cargo Ship Rescue breakout
grade6.lead: The key words for Grade 6 science and the Cargo Ship Rescue breakout — in plain language, with an example for each. Keep this open while you solve the locks.
grade6.footer: Science Critical Thinking Breakouts · Grade 6 · Self-contained, no logins, no data collected.
grade6.dd.0: Anything that has mass and takes up space.Example: air, water, a steel crate — all matter.
grade6.dd.1: How much "stuff" is in an object. We measure it in grams or kilograms.Example: a loaded crate has more mass than an empty one.
grade6.dd.2: How much space an object takes up.Example: a big hollow hull has a large volume.
grade6.dd.3: How tightly mass is packed into a space. Density = mass ÷ volume.Example: a steel bar is very dense; foam is not.
grade6.dd.4: A liquid or gas that can flow, like water or air.Example: a ship floats in the fluid we call water.
grade6.dd.5: An object floats when its overall density is less than the fluid's, and sinks when it is more.Example: a hollow ship floats; a solid bar sinks.
grade6.dd.6: Two or more materials mixed together but not chemically joined.Example: sand stirred into water.
grade6.dd.7: A change that makes a new substance. Clues include a gas, a color change, heat, or a solid forming.Example: iron rusting.
grade6.dd.8: A push or a pull on an object.Example: a wave pushing a crate sideways.
grade6.dd.9: The force that pulls objects down toward Earth.Example: gravity pulls the crate onto the deck.
grade6.dd.10: A force that resists sliding when two surfaces rub.Example: friction keeps the crate from sliding at a small nudge.
grade6.dd.11: The upward push a surface gives to an object resting on it.Example: the deck pushes up on the crate.
grade6.dd.12: The total force left over after you add up all the forces on an object.Example: if pushes cancel out, the net force is zero.
grade6.dd.13: Forces that add up to zero, so the object's motion does not change.Example: a crate sitting still on the deck.
grade6.dd.14: Forces that do not add up to zero, so the object speeds up, slows down, or changes direction.Example: a wave's extra push makes the crate slide.
grade6.dd.15: For every force there is an equal and opposite force on the other object.Example: the propeller pushes water back; the water pushes the ship forward.
grade6.dd.16: The ability to make something move or change.Example: the crane uses energy to lift a crate.
grade6.dd.17: Stored energy, ready to be used. A lifted object has gravitational potential energy.Example: a crate held high by the crane.
grade6.dd.18: The energy of a moving object.Example: the crate speeding up as it lowers.
grade6.dd.19: Energy moving from one object or form to another.Example: electrical energy becomes motion.
grade6.dd.20: Energy is never created or destroyed. It only changes form or moves.Example: the crane's energy is never "used up" — it changes form.

grade7.crumb: ‹ Grade 7 Science · Rescue Run breakout
grade7.lead: The key words for Grade 7 science and the Rescue Run breakout — in plain language, with an example for each. Keep this open while you solve the locks.
grade7.footer: Science Critical Thinking Breakouts · Grade 7 · Self-contained, no logins, no data collected.
grade7.dd.0: How fast something moves. Speed = distance ÷ time.Example: a drone flying 12 km in one hour has a speed of 12 km/h.
grade7.dd.1: The total distance divided by the total time for a whole trip.Example: 6 km in 30 minutes is an average speed of 12 km/h.
grade7.dd.2: Speed plus a direction.Example: 12 km/h heading north.
grade7.dd.3: The straight-line distance and direction from start to finish. It is zero if you end where you began.Example: fly out and loop back to base → displacement is zero.
grade7.dd.4: A graph that shows how far something is from the start over time.Example: a rising line means moving away.
grade7.dd.5: How steep a line is on a graph. On a distance–time graph, a steeper slope means faster speed; a flat line means stopped.Example: a flat line = the drone is hovering.
grade7.dd.6: The energy of moving particles that we feel as heat.Example: hot desert air has a lot of thermal energy.
grade7.dd.7: A measure of the average motion (kinetic energy) of an object's particles.Example: a higher temperature means faster-moving particles.
grade7.dd.8: Heat moving from a warmer place to a cooler place.Example: heat moving from hot air into a cold cooler.
grade7.dd.9: Heat moving by direct touch between materials.Example: a metal spoon getting hot in soup.
grade7.dd.10: Heat carried by moving liquids or gases.Example: warm air rising off the sand.
grade7.dd.11: Heat that travels as rays, even through empty space.Example: heat from the Sun.
grade7.dd.12: When two things reach the same temperature and heat stops flowing between them.Example: a drink and its melting ice ending at the same temperature.
grade7.dd.13: A material that slows heat transfer. It cannot add cold or stop heat forever.Example: foam or cotton in a cooler.
grade7.dd.14: A diagram showing that only about 10% of energy passes to the next level of a food chain.Example: grass → grasshopper → bird loses energy at each step.
grade7.dd.15: A step in a food chain, such as producers, then plant-eaters, then meat-eaters.Example: a hawk is at a high trophic level.

grade8.dd.0: The tiny building block that all matter is made of.Example: water is made of hydrogen and oxygen atoms.
grade8.dd.1: A pure substance made of just one kind of atom.Example: oxygen, iron, gold.
grade8.dd.2: A substance made of two or more kinds of atoms joined together.Example: water (H₂O) is a compound.
grade8.dd.3: A change where atoms rearrange to form new substances.Example: baking soda and vinegar fizzing.
grade8.dd.4: Reactants are what you start with; products are what you end with.Example: vinegar + baking soda → gas + liquid.
grade8.dd.5: In a chemical reaction, atoms are only rearranged, so the total mass before equals the total mass after.Example: a sealed bag weighs the same before and after it fizzes.
grade8.dd.6: A container where nothing can enter or leave.Example: a zip-sealed reaction bag keeps every atom inside.
grade8.dd.7: A push or a pull, measured in newtons (N).Example: a rocket engine's thrust.
grade8.dd.8: The total force left after adding up all the forces on an object.Example: thrust minus drag and gravity.
grade8.dd.9: How much matter is in an object.Example: adding cargo increases a rocket's mass.
grade8.dd.10: How quickly an object's velocity changes (speeding up, slowing down, or turning).Example: a rocket gaining speed at liftoff.
grade8.dd.11: Acceleration = net force ÷ mass (a = F ÷ m). For the same force, more mass means less acceleration.Example: a heavier rocket accelerates more slowly.
grade8.dd.12: A disturbance that carries energy from one place to another.Example: a radio wave carrying data.
grade8.dd.13: The height of a wave — how much energy it carries.Example: a taller wave carries more energy.
grade8.dd.14: The distance from one wave crest to the next.Example: radio waves have long wavelengths.
grade8.dd.15: How many waves pass a point each second.Example: higher frequency means a shorter wavelength.
grade8.dd.16: A wave that can travel through empty space, like light, radio, or X-rays.Example: telemetry signals from a rocket.
